Note::TexAccessor::to_latex¶

Back to Note TeX Accessor API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::TexAccessor::to_latex(std::int64_t mode = 0) const

Convert Plain Text Toward TeX Source¶

to_latex() is the opposite direction from to_text and render: where those reduce authored TeX down to plain text or Unicode, to_latex() builds TeX source up from plain text. It escapes every cell the same way escape does, then — depending on mode — maps common math words and comparison operators to their TeX commands and wraps the result in $...$ when it looks like a formula.

Unlike to_text’s and to_markdown’s mode, this one is validated: only 0, 1, and 2 are accepted, and any other value — including negative numbers, which to_text’s mode treats as 0 — is rejected.

mode¶

  • 0 (the default) — escape only, exactly escape()’s ten-character table. No word or operator mapping, no wrapping.

  • 1 — escape, then map recognized math words (alpha → \alpha, infty/inf → \infty, sqrt → \sqrt, and similar) and comparison operators (<= → \leq , >= → \geq , != → \neq , -> → \to , and related arrows/signs), then collapse and trim whitespace. A sqrt(...) call is additionally rewritten to \sqrt{...} braces.

  • 2 — everything 1 does, and additionally wraps the result in $...$ when it looks like a formula: the escaped/mapped text contains a backslash (any \command, from mode 1’s own mapping or already present in the source) or one of = + - * / ^ _ < >. A cell with none of those — ordinary prose — is left unwrapped even at mode 2.

The operation is shape-preserving, cell-independent, and returns a fresh Note. Undefined input remains undefined; Bool, Int64, Float64, and Bytes receivers are rejected because the input is treated as plain text.

Example 1: All Three Modes On The Same Source¶

const auto source = pluss::make_note(
    {"x_1 & 50% complete", "alpha + beta <= gamma",
     "plain words", "sqrt(x) -> infty"});
std::cout << source.tex().to_latex(0) << '\n';
std::cout << source.tex().to_latex(1) << '\n';
std::cout << source.tex().to_latex(2) << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["x\\_1 \\& 50\\% complete", "alpha + beta <= gamma", "plain words", "sqrt(x) -> infty"]
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["x\\_1 \\& 50\\% complete", "\\alpha + \\beta \\leq \\gamma", "plain words", "\\sqrt{x} \\to \\infty"]
Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["$x\\_1 \\& 50\\% complete$", "$\\alpha + \\beta \\leq \\gamma$", "plain words", "$\\sqrt{x} \\to \\infty$"]

At mode 0, only the special characters are escaped — alpha, <=, and sqrt(x) -> infty are untouched. At mode 1, the words and operators map to commands. At mode 2, every cell whose mapped text contains \ or one of =+-*/^_<> gets wrapped in $...$ — three of the four do; "plain words" has neither and stays bare even though it went through the same mode-2 call.

Example 2: A 2-D Grid At The Default Mode¶

const auto grid = pluss::make_note(
    std::vector<std::string>{"a_b", "alpha", "x+y", ""},
    std::array<std::int64_t, 2>{2, 2});
std::cout << grid.tex().to_latex() << '\n';

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["a\\_b", "alpha"], 
  ["x+y", ""]
]

to_latex() with no argument is mode 0: a_b is escaped to a\_b, but alpha is left as the literal word (mode 0 does no word mapping).

Example 3: An Out-Of-Range Mode Is Rejected¶

for (const auto mode : {-1, 3}) {
  try {
    (void)source.tex().to_latex(mode);
  } catch (const pluss::Error&) {
    std::cout << "to_latex(" << mode << "): rejected\n";
  }
}

Output¶

to_latex(-1): rejected
to_latex(3): rejected

Only 0, 1, and 2 are valid; every other integer, including negative values, is rejected before the receiver is read.

Example 4: Undefined And Non-Text Input¶

std::cout << std::boolalpha
          << pluss::Note::undefined().tex().to_latex().defined() << '\n';
try {
  (void)pluss::note::make(std::vector<std::int64_t>{1, 2}).tex().to_latex();
} catch (const pluss::Error&) {
  std::cout << "to latex Int64: rejected\n";
}

Output¶

false
to latex Int64: rejected

See Also¶

  • escape: exactly to_latex(0)’s special-character table, callable on its own.

  • to_text: the inverse direction — reduce authored TeX to plain text.

  • render: render TeX toward readable Unicode instead of building TeX source.
